data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: The dinar is pegged to an undisclosed basket (heavily dollar-weighted), and inflation has been low and stable where measured: 2.9% in 2014, easing to 0.6% in 2018, then 4.0% in 2022 on the global shock, with the IMF projecting 2.4% for 2025. Note the IMF series has no inflation data for 2006-13, a genuine data gap. Subsidized fuel, food, and utilities dampen pass-through, and the central bank shadows external monetary conditions. Price stability has never been the problem; fiscal policy has.
debt_management: Kuwait barely borrowed for most of the period: debt fell from 7.8% of GDP in 2006 to just 2.9% by 2024, as oil surpluses funded the state. But the 2014-16 oil crash exposed the model: with parliament blocking both the debt law and reforms, the government drained the General Reserve Fund until it faced a liquidity crunch in 2020. A new debt law was finally passed in 2025, and the IMF projects debt jumping to 14.6% that year as Kuwait returns to bond markets. The sovereign wealth (Future Generations Fund) remains enormous, so solvency is not at issue, but the episode showed institutional paralysis.

key_events.event: Oil boom took GDP to $147.4bn; the crisis then halved it by 2009.
Arab Spring-era handouts expanded the public wage bill structurally.
Oil crash; deficits began and the reserve drain started.
COVID and the oil collapse; General Reserve Fund liquidity crunch forced asset maneuvers.
Oil windfall (GDP $183.5bn) papered over the unresolved fiscal impasse.
New public debt law passed; IMF projects debt at 14.6% of GDP as borrowing resumes.

outlook_next_decade: Kuwait's finances are strong in assets but weak in institutions: the wealth funds guarantee solvency, yet without subsidy and public-sector reform, deficits return whenever oil dips. The 2025 debt law gives breathing room, not a solution. Upside from the northern oil fields and diversification projects exists but has been promised for decades. Analytical assessment: expect continued stop-start reform with fiscal crises recurring on each oil downturn until structural spending is addressed.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
